$$

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$

$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}+{1}^{2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1 \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-1,1)} & =3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+(1){e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =3+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)={cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(0,\sqrt{\pi }).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({cos}^{2}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (3x\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})) \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\cdot (3x\cdot 0-2y) \\  & =4y\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,\sqrt{\pi }):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(0,\sqrt{\pi })} & =4(\sqrt{\pi })\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(0)-{(\sqrt{\pi })}^{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(0)-{(\sqrt{\pi })}^{2}) \\  & =4\sqrt{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=(2y+1)^{2x+1},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(2,0).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((2y+1)^{2x+1}) \\  & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}((2y+1))\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot (2\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\cdot (2\cdot 1+0) \\  & =2(2x+1)(2y+1)^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,0)} & =2\cdot (2\cdot 2+1)\cdot (2\cdot 0+1)^{2\cdot 2} \\  & =2\cdot 5\cdot {1}^{4} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)-xy) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx) & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)-\frac{∂}{∂x}(yx) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1-y\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{x}-y\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,3).$
:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{(x{y}^{2})}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the constant multiple rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{1+{x}^{2}{y}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,3)} & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{1+{1}^{2}\cdot {3}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{9}{1+81} \\  & =\frac{9}{82}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y}+{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the chain and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x+y})+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y))+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot (0+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(3,1) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3+1}}+\frac{{3}^{2}}{2\sqrt{1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differenciation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot (2x+{y}^{2}\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\sqrt{3}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
